title: Non-Desarguesian Planes: The Moulton Plane Counterexample
description: Formalizes the Moulton plane (1902) — a non-Desarguesian affine plane over ℝ — and provides an explicit rational-coordinate counterexample showing that Desargues's theorem fails. Two triangles are in perspective from a point yet their corresponding-side intersections are not Moulton-collinear.

overview.historicalContext:
Girard Desargues (1591–1661), a Lyonnais architect and engineer in the orbit of Marin Mersenne, proved his perspective-triangle theorem c. 1639 in his now-rare *Brouillon project d'une atteinte aux événements des rencontres du cône avec un plan* (a small print run, of which most copies were lost; the work was reconstructed in the 19th century from a single surviving copy and from Philippe de la Hire's 1679 paraphrase). The theorem was first published as a stand-alone result by Abraham Bosse in *Manière universelle de M. Desargues pour pratiquer la perspective* (1648) and was rediscovered in the 19th century by Jean-Victor Poncelet (*Traité des propriétés projectives des figures*, 1822). In its modern form Desargues's theorem asserts: if triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are *perspective from a point* — that is, the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ all meet at a common point $O$ — then the three intersection points $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are *collinear*. The theorem is self-dual, an instance of the duality principle that converts every projective theorem about points and lines into one about lines and points (formalized in this gallery's `desargues-theorem-oq-04`).

For over two centuries, Desargues's theorem was treated as a deductive consequence of the plane projective axioms (incidence, line-uniqueness, point-uniqueness). The shift came with David Hilbert's *Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899) — the foundational text that made axiomatic independence a central question of geometry. Hilbert systematically asked, for each classical theorem, *which* axioms it depends on, and in §§22–30 of *Grundlagen* he proved that Desargues's theorem is necessary for the introduction of coordinates from a skew field (division ring) into a projective plane: any 'Desarguesian' projective plane (one in which the theorem holds) can be coordinatized by a unique-up-to-isomorphism skew field, and conversely. This left open the question whether every projective plane *was* Desarguesian — i.e., whether the theorem followed from incidence axioms alone.

Forest Ray Moulton (1872–1952), a University of Chicago astronomer and applied mathematician (best known for the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis of solar-system formation and for editing the *Astronomical Journal* 1947–1952), settled the question in his 4-page paper *A Simple Non-Desarguesian Plane Geometry* (Trans. AMS, vol. 3, no. 2, 1902, pp. 192–195) — written while Moulton was a graduate student of E. H. Moore. Moulton's construction is the minimal perturbation of the Euclidean plane that breaks Desargues: take the points of $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the lines of $\mathbb{R}^2$ *except* those with positive slope, which are 'bent' at the $y$-axis so that the right half has half the slope of the left half. All affine plane axioms remain satisfied (two points determine a unique Moulton line; two non-parallel Moulton lines meet in a unique point; the parallel postulate holds), yet Desargues fails for explicit rational-coordinate triangles. The Moulton plane was the first 'non-Desarguesian' affine plane and established a fundamental distinction in projective geometry: between planes coordinatizable by a skew field (where Desargues holds) and planes requiring weaker algebraic structures (where it fails).

The theory developed rapidly after Moulton. Gerhard Hessenberg (1874–1925) proved in 1905 (*Math. Ann.*, vol. 61, pp. 161–172) that *Pappus's theorem implies Desargues's theorem* — a Pappian plane is automatically Desarguesian, so the Moulton plane cannot satisfy Pappus either. Oswald Veblen and John Wesley Young, in *Projective Geometry* (vol. 1, 1910) and Veblen's 1908 *Annals of Mathematics* paper, proved that in projective *spaces* of dimension $\geq 3$, Desargues's theorem follows automatically from the incidence axioms — the pathology is intrinsically a plane phenomenon. Marshall Hall, Jr. (1910–1990) constructed the first finite non-Desarguesian projective plane in 1943 (*Trans. AMS*, vol. 54, pp. 229–277): the **Hall plane** of order 9, with $9^2 + 9 + 1 = 91$ points and 91 lines, coordinatized by a non-associative *nearfield* of order 9. Daniel Hughes constructed a different infinite family in 1957 (*Math. Z.*, vol. 67, pp. 251–262). For finite planes, the Bruck-Ryser theorem (1949) gives necessary conditions on the order $n$, and the Lam-Thiel-Swiercz computer-aided proof (1989) ruled out order 10 entirely. The classification of non-Desarguesian planes remains a major open program in finite geometry. The Moulton plane sits at the historical beginning of this story — a simple, explicit, real-coordinate counterexample whose 2-page argument the present 297-line Lean formalization makes machine-checkable, axiom-free, and tractable with modern tactic automation.
overview.problemStatement: Can we formalize non-Desarguesian projective planes in Lean to show when Desargues's theorem fails? Desargues's theorem asserts: if triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are in perspective from a point (i.e., lines $OAA'$, $OBB'$, $OCC'$ are concurrent at $O$), then the corresponding-side intersections $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are collinear. The Moulton plane (1902) satisfies all affine plane axioms but violates Desargues: `desargues_fails : ¬ MoultonCollinear P_pt Q_pt R_pt`.
overview.proofStrategy:
The formalization realises Moulton's 1902 4-page proof in six structural stages, each implementing one of the conceptual ingredients of the original argument as a self-contained Lean module.

**Stage 1 — Define the bent-line predicate.** `onMoultonLine m b P` is built as a two-level `Classical` if-then-else: ordinary line $y = mx + b$ when $m \leq 0$, bent line (slope $m$ on $x \leq 0$, slope $m/2$ on $x > 0$) when $m > 0$. `MoultonCollinear P Q R` is *disjunctive*: either all three points share an $x$-coordinate (vertical line) or there exist $(m, b)$ with all three on the same Moulton line. The disjunctive shape is forced by the slope-intercept formalism (vertical lines have undefined slope), and it directly drives the three-case structure of the main non-collinearity proof downstream.

**Stage 2 — Expose constructors and extractors.** Six helper lemmas (`onML_neg_slope`, `onML_pos_left`, `onML_pos_right` and their three `_eq_` extractors) bridge the predicate form and the bare linear equation. Without them, every downstream proof would have to unfold the if-then-else inside `linarith` or `ring`, slowing automation and obscuring the math. The split lets the perspectivity and intersection blocks be uniformly one-liners of the shape `helper (by norm_num) _ (by simp […]; ring)`.

**Stage 3 — Verify the perspectivity hypothesis.** The triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are chosen so that $A' = 2A$, $B' = 3B$, $C' = 4C$ — distinct scalar multiples of the original triangle from $O = (0, 0)$. This makes perspectivity from $O$ algebraically immediate (each pair $O, A_i, A'_i$ lies on a ray through $O$), and the three lemmas `collinear_OAA'`, `collinear_OBB'`, `collinear_OCC'` discharge the hypothesis using all three branches of `MoultonCollinear`: negative-slope ordinary line for $OAA'$, positive-slope bent line for $OBB'$, vertical line for $OCC'$. The *distinct* scaling factors $2, 3, 4$ are essential — equal factors would make the corresponding sides parallel and send the intersection points to infinity, trivialising the question.

**Stage 4 — Verify the side incidences.** Eighteen lemmas pin down $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$ as the Moulton-line intersections of the corresponding sides. Sides $AB, A'B', CA, C'A'$ all have negative slope (ordinary Moulton lines, bending invisible), so the $P$ and $R$ blocks use `onML_neg_slope` exclusively. Sides $BC, B'C'$ have positive slope (left-slopes $4/3, 14/9$), so the $Q$ block exercises both `onML_pos_left` (for $C, C'$ on the seam $x = 0$) and `onML_pos_right` (for $Q, B, B'$ on the right half). This deliberate asymmetry — ordinary lines through $P, R$, bent lines through $Q$ — is the proof-architectural setup that makes the bend detectable in stage 5.

**Stage 5 — Refute Moulton-collinearity of $P, Q, R$.** Tactic-mode `desargues_fails` is the heart of the formalization. After `rcases` peels off the two disjuncts of `MoultonCollinear`, the vertical case is closed by $-17 \neq 27$ via `norm_num`. `by_cases hm : m ≤ 0` then splits the non-vertical case. The negative-slope leaf computes the Euclidean slope of $PQ$ as $\tfrac{17 - 9}{27 - (-17)} = \tfrac{8}{44} = \tfrac{2}{11} > 0$, contradicting $m \leq 0$ via `linarith`. The positive-slope leaf uses the bent definition: $P, R$ on left-half give $9 = -17m + b$ and $11 = -6m + b$ (`onML_eq_pos_left`), while $Q$ on right-half gives $17 = \tfrac{m}{2} \cdot 27 + b$ (`onML_eq_pos_right`, with the halved slope!). Two `linear_combination` invocations (`hP' - hR'` and `2 hP' - 2 hQ'`) eliminate $b$ and produce $11m = 2$ and $61m = 16$, an over-determined system in $m$ with no solution (the cross-multiplied check $61 \cdot 2 = 122 \neq 176 = 11 \cdot 16$ closes via `linarith`).

**Stage 6 — Assemble the counterexample certificate.** `moulton_counterexample` is a 22-component conjunction packaging perspectivity, the 18 side incidences, and `desargues_fails` into a single citable theorem statement, proven by a one-line anonymous constructor `⟨…⟩` referencing the 22 prior lemmas. This makes the Moulton failure of Desargues a *citable mathematical object* for downstream formalizations of the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization correspondence, the Veblen-Young dimension dichotomy, or other classifications of non-Desarguesian planes.

The entire formalization invokes only five tactics — `norm_num`, `linarith`, `linear_combination`, `by_cases`, `simp` (plus the term-mode `ring` for closing linear-equation goals) — and uses no Mathlib structures beyond `ℝ × ℝ` and the standard arithmetic tactics. No topology, no continuity, no algebraic geometry, no projective-plane infrastructure: pure elementary algebra on rational points in the affine plane. This minimalism is deliberate — it demonstrates that combinatorial-geometric counterexamples are tractable in modern Lean 4 at the 300-line scale with essentially no specialised infrastructure, and it positions the formalization as a building block that any downstream projective-geometry formalization can incorporate without inheriting heavy dependencies.
keyInsights: **The bending rule is the minimal perturbation that breaks Desargues while preserving all affine plane axioms.** Moulton's 1902 insight was that the line geometry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be modified by a single piecewise rule — slope $m$ on $x \leq 0$, slope $m/2$ on $x > 0$, only for positive-slope lines — to break Desargues without disturbing any of the three classical affine axioms. (1) *Two-points determine a unique line*: for any two distinct points $P, Q \in \mathbb{R}^2$, the Moulton line through them is uniquely specified by their relative positions (vertical if $P_x = Q_x$; ordinary Euclidean line if both points are on the same half-plane and the resulting slope is $\leq 0$; bent line with the appropriately reconstructed left-slope otherwise). (2) *Two non-parallel lines meet in a unique point*: solving the bent-line equations across the seam $x = 0$ always yields a unique intersection. (3) *Parallel postulate (Playfair)*: through any point not on a given Moulton line, there is exactly one Moulton line parallel to it (using the natural left-slope-equality definition of parallelism). What the bend *does* break is the perspective-triangles property: the seam $x = 0$ creates an asymmetry between the half-planes that prevents the standard linear-algebra closure used to prove Desargues over $\mathbb{R}$. The choice of factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ for the right-half slope is the simplest rational coefficient that achieves this — any $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ with $\lambda \neq 1$ would also work (see keyInsight #9), but $\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}$ admits the cleanest rational-coordinate counterexamples and was Moulton's canonical choice in the 1902 paper.

**$P$ and $R$ live in the ordinary regime; only $Q$ exercises the bend.** Sides $AB$ (slope $-2/5$), $A'B'$ (slope $-3/13$), $CA$ (slope $-2$), and $C'A'$ (slope $-5/2$) all have *negative* slope, so they are unmodified Euclidean lines in the Moulton plane and the intersection points $P = AB \cap A'B' = (-17, 9)$ and $R = CA \cap C'A' = (-6, 11)$ are computed by ordinary slope-intercept linear algebra. Only the third intersection $Q = BC \cap B'C'$ is affected by the bend: sides $BC$ and $B'C'$ have positive Euclidean slopes ($2/3$ and $7/9$), so as Moulton lines they parametrise by left-slopes $4/3$ and $14/9$ respectively (twice the Euclidean slope, since the right half halves the left), and $Q = (27, 17)$ at $x = 27 > 0$ sits on the *right half-plane* where the halved slope applies. The bend is therefore invisible during the construction of $P, Q, R$ — each is computed correctly by classical methods — and becomes visible *only* when the three points are tested for joint Moulton-collinearity in `desargues_fails`. This asymmetry is the proof-architectural reason the counterexample works: any attempted Moulton line through $P, Q, R$ would have to be positive-slope (since $P$ and $Q$ have slope $\tfrac{8}{44} > 0$ in the Euclidean reading), would use its left-half equation for $P, R$ (both at $x < 0$) and its right-half equation for $Q$ (at $x > 0$), and the regime mismatch over-determines $(m, b)$. Removing the bend (i.e. setting $\lambda = 1$) would let the same line equation work in both half-planes and Desargues would hold, exactly as it does in the underlying Euclidean plane.

**The contradiction reduces to an over-determined $2 \times 2$ linear system in $(m, b)$.** Assuming Moulton-collinearity of $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$ on a positive-slope bent line with left-slope $m$ and intercept $b$ produces three equations: $9 = -17m + b$ from $P$ at $x < 0$ (left-half slope), $17 = \tfrac{m}{2} \cdot 27 + b$ from $Q$ at $x > 0$ (right-half *halved* slope), and $11 = -6m + b$ from $R$ at $x < 0$ (left-half slope). The pair $(P, R)$ uses only the left-half equation, so subtracting gives $-2 = -11m$ and hence $m = \tfrac{2}{11}$; the pair $(P, Q)$ mixes regimes, and after clearing the half-factor by doubling ($2 \cdot \mathrm{hP'} - 2 \cdot \mathrm{hQ'}$) yields $-16 = -61m$ and hence $m = \tfrac{16}{61}$. The two values of $m$ are incompatible: $\tfrac{2}{11} = \tfrac{122}{671}$ while $\tfrac{16}{61} = \tfrac{176}{671}$. Lean's `linarith` closes the goal by detecting $61 \cdot 2 = 122 \neq 176 = 11 \cdot 16$, which is integer-arithmetic-decidable. This is a deeply *algebraic* obstruction, not a geometric or topological one — at the structural level, the bent definition makes the affine plane fail to satisfy the cross-ratio invariance that an ordinary projective-coordinate proof of Desargues exploits, and the over-determination of the linear system is the local manifestation of that global failure. The proof has no recourse to compactness, continuity, or topological completeness — pure rational linear algebra suffices, which is why the Lean formalization needs only `norm_num`, `linarith`, and `linear_combination`.

**$P, Q, R$ are Euclidean-collinear, confirming that classical Desargues holds in $\mathbb{R}^2$ — the failure is created by the bend alone.** A direct computation in the Euclidean plane shows that the slope from $P = (-17, 9)$ to $Q = (27, 17)$ is $\tfrac{17 - 9}{27 - (-17)} = \tfrac{8}{44} = \tfrac{2}{11}$ and the slope from $P$ to $R = (-6, 11)$ is $\tfrac{11 - 9}{-6 - (-17)} = \tfrac{2}{11}$ — the same slope. The Euclidean line through all three is $y = \tfrac{2}{11} x + \tfrac{121}{11}$ (the intercept follows from $9 = \tfrac{2}{11} \cdot (-17) + b$, i.e. $b = 9 + \tfrac{34}{11} = \tfrac{121}{11}$). This confirms two things at once: (i) classical Desargues holds in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as it must (the Euclidean plane is coordinatised by the field $\mathbb{R}$, hence Pappian and Desarguesian by the Hilbert-Hall correspondence), and (ii) the Moulton failure is created *purely* by the choice of which lines count — the bent positive-slope line that would be needed to witness Moulton-collinearity of $P, Q, R$ simply does not exist in the Moulton family, even though the corresponding ordinary Euclidean line through them does exist. The contrast is the cleanest possible illustration of how axiomatic geometry decouples 'the points and lines of $\mathbb{R}^2$' from 'the affine plane structure on those points': the *point-set* is identical between the Euclidean and Moulton planes, but the *line-set* is changed by the bending rule, and Desargues is a fact about lines, not points.

Characterisation: Desargues's theorem holds in a projective plane iff the plane is coordinatizable by a skew field (division ring) — the Moulton plane's bent coordinatization is not associative, blocking this coordinatization

**Hessenberg's theorem (1905): Pappus implies Desargues.** Pappus's hexagon theorem — for points $A_1, A_2, A_3$ on one line and $B_1, B_2, B_3$ on another, the three intersections $A_1B_2 \cap A_2B_1$, $A_1B_3 \cap A_3B_1$, $A_2B_3 \cap A_3B_2$ are collinear — is *strictly stronger* than Desargues. Hessenberg's 1905 proof (*Math. Ann.* 61) shows that Pappus + incidence axioms $\Rightarrow$ Desargues, so every Pappian plane is Desarguesian. The converse fails: Hilbert exhibited Desarguesian-but-not-Pappian planes using division rings that are non-commutative (e.g., the quaternions). The Pappus/Desargues asymmetry corresponds exactly to the field/skew-field asymmetry under coordinatization: a projective plane is Desarguesian iff it is coordinatizable by a skew field, and *additionally* Pappian iff that skew field is commutative. By Wedderburn's little theorem (1905) — every finite skew field is a field — finite Desarguesian planes are automatically Pappian, so non-Pappian Desarguesian planes must be infinite (the simplest example uses the real quaternions $\mathbb{H}$). The Moulton plane, being non-Desarguesian, is *a fortiori* non-Pappian — but the more interesting separation (Desarguesian but non-Pappian) requires infinite skew fields. Hessenberg's theorem is the structural reason: commutativity is a stronger algebraic property than associativity, mirrored in projective geometry as Pappus being strictly stronger than Desargues.

**The dimension-2 vs dimension-$\geq 3$ dichotomy (Veblen-Young, 1908–1910).** Desargues's theorem is *automatic* in projective spaces of dimension $\geq 3$: Veblen and Young proved that in any projective space satisfying the basic incidence axioms with at least three independent points off any plane, Desargues's theorem holds for free. The proof is the classical 3-dimensional argument — when two perspective triangles lie in distinct planes, the three intersection points are forced to lie on the line of intersection of those two planes; the planar case is recovered by an embedding argument when a third plane is available. The pathology that produces Moulton-style counterexamples is therefore intrinsically two-dimensional: in dimension $\geq 3$, the ambient space supplies enough 'room' to force Desarguesian behaviour combinatorially, and non-Desarguesian projective spaces of dimension $\geq 3$ simply do not exist. This is why classical algebraic geometry — which works in $\mathbb{P}^n$ for $n \geq 2$ but typically embeds the plane case into higher-dimensional ambient spaces — never encounters the Moulton-plane pathology. The Lean formalization here exploits this asymmetry implicitly: the Moulton construction is *defined* on $\mathbb{R}^2$ rather than on any $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \geq 3$, because the bending trick has no $n \geq 3$ analogue. Together with Hessenberg's theorem, the dimension-2 / dimension-$\geq 3$ dichotomy completes the structural picture: Desargues is automatic above dimension 2, equivalent to skew-field coordinatization at dimension 2, and refutable by bent-line constructions like Moulton's once we stay genuinely planar.

**Coordinatization by ternary rings and the Hall plane (1943).** Marshall Hall, Jr. (*Trans. AMS*, vol. 54, 1943) showed that *every* projective plane — Desarguesian or not — can be coordinatized by an algebraic structure called a **planar ternary ring** (PTR): a set $R$ with a ternary operation $T(x, y, z) = xy + z$ satisfying axioms abstracted from the incidence behaviour of slopes and intercepts. The coordinatization hierarchy is then strictly graded: a projective plane is (i) coordinatizable by a PTR (always), (ii) Desarguesian iff coordinatizable by a skew field (Hilbert 1899, Hall 1943), (iii) Moufang — i.e. satisfying the 'little Desargues' theorem where the perspective point lies on one of the corresponding sides — iff coordinatizable by an *alternative algebra* (which by Bruck-Kleinfeld is either a skew field or a Cayley-Dickson algebra; the only Moufang plane not Desarguesian is the real Cayley plane $\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^2$ over the octonions), and (iv) Pappian iff coordinatizable by a commutative field. The Moulton plane is at the bottom of this hierarchy: its planar ternary ring is genuinely non-associative and not even Moufang. The smallest *finite* non-Desarguesian plane is the **Hall plane of order 9** (Hall 1943), with $9^2 + 9 + 1 = 91$ points and 91 lines, coordinatized by a non-associative *nearfield* of order 9 (Dickson 1905) — the same nearfield that André's 1954 generalization uses to produce a non-Desarguesian plane of every prime-power order $p^{2k}$ for $p$ odd. Beyond the Hall family, the Hughes plane (1957) gives a different construction for orders $p^2$ with $p$ odd prime, and the Bruck-Ryser-Chowla theorem (1949–1950) plus the Lam-Thiel-Swiercz computer search (1989) ruled out orders 6 and 10 entirely. The Moulton plane is the historical and conceptual prototype that opened this entire program; the Lean formalization here makes its 2-page 1902 argument fully machine-checkable in the 21st-century Lean 4 ecosystem.

**Why the bend is exactly halved: the unique minimal perturbation.** The Moulton line definition uses slope $m$ for $x \leq 0$ and slope $m/2$ for $x > 0$ when $m > 0$ — but why the factor $1/2$ specifically? Any continuous piecewise-linear bending with two different positive slopes works: replacing $m/2$ by any $\lambda m$ with $0 < \lambda < 1$ gives a different non-Desarguesian plane, and the Lean counterexample data ($A = (-2,3)$, $B = (3,1)$, etc., yielding $P = (-17,9)$, $Q = (27,17)$, $R = (-6,11)$) would need to be re-tuned to maintain non-collinearity. Moulton's original 1902 choice of $\lambda = 1/2$ is the *simplest* rational factor that breaks Desargues — and the specific rational coordinates of the counterexample are tuned to this $\lambda$. Trying $\lambda = 1$ recovers the ordinary Euclidean plane (Desargues holds), $\lambda = 0$ collapses positive-slope right-half-plane lines to horizontals (incidence axioms fail), and any irrational $\lambda$ would prevent rational-coordinate counterexamples like the present one. The choice $\lambda = 1/2$ is the Goldilocks zone — small enough to break the structural symmetry that Desargues requires, large enough to preserve incidence and parallel axioms, and rational enough to admit clean rational-coordinate witnesses. The algebraic explanation: under Hall's PTR coordinatization, the choice $\lambda = 1/2$ produces a ternary ring whose multiplication on positive elements is not associative — specifically, the failure $a \cdot (b \cdot c) \neq (a \cdot b) \cdot c$ for positive $a, b, c$ near the $y$-axis is what blocks the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization-by-skew-field that Desargues requires. Other $\lambda \in (0,1)$ values give isomorphic non-Desarguesian planes — the family is topologically a 1-parameter deformation, but $\lambda = 1/2$ is the canonical representative for arithmetic reasons.
prerequisites: Affine and projective plane axioms: two-points-determine-a-line, two-non-parallel-lines-meet-in-a-point, parallel postulate (in the affine case), and the distinction between affine and projective completions (line at infinity)

Desargues's theorem: triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are *perspective from a point* $O$ (i.e., lines $OAA'$, $OBB'$, $OCC'$ concurrent) iff they are *perspective from a line* (the three intersections $P = AB \cap A'B'$, $Q = BC \cap B'C'$, $R = CA \cap C'A'$ are collinear) — see `desargues-theorem` for the standard $\mathbb{R}^3$ homogeneous-coordinate proof

Coordinatization theory: the Hilbert-Hall correspondence between geometric axioms and algebraic structures on the coordinatizing ring — Pappian $\Leftrightarrow$ commutative field, Desarguesian $\Leftrightarrow$ skew field (division ring), Moufang $\Leftrightarrow$ alternative algebra, general projective plane $\Leftrightarrow$ planar ternary ring (Hall 1943)

Hessenberg's theorem (1905): Pappus $\Rightarrow$ Desargues, giving the strict hierarchy Pappian $\subsetneq$ Desarguesian $\subsetneq$ all planes (the converse failing via non-commutative division rings like the real quaternions $\mathbb{H}$)

Wedderburn's little theorem (1905): every finite division ring is commutative, equivalently every finite Desarguesian projective plane is Pappian — so finite non-Desarguesian planes (Hall plane of order 9, Hughes planes, André planes) are the only finite witnesses for the strict containment Pappian $\subsetneq$ Desarguesian

Lean 4 piecewise-definition idioms: `Classical.propDecidable` to enable `if-then-else` on `Prop` (needed for the Moulton-line slope-sign case split), `by_cases h : m ≤ 0` for tactic-mode case analysis, and the `norm_num` / `linarith` / `linear_combination` arithmetic tactics that close every numeric goal in the 297-line formalization

Rational-coordinate linear algebra in $\mathbb{Q}^2$: explicit computation of line intersections via the slope-intercept formulas $y = mx + b$ and $y = m'x + b'$, the cross-product collinearity test $\det\!\begin{pmatrix} x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 \\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 \end{pmatrix} = 0$, and the numeric witnesses $A = (-2, 3)$, $B = (3, 1)$, $C = (0, -1)$, $A' = (-4, 6)$, $B' = (9, 3)$, $C' = (0, -4)$ that produce the explicit counterexample $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$

mainTheorems.name: onMoultonLine
mainTheorems.description: The piecewise Moulton line predicate. For slope m ≤ 0: ordinary line y = mx + b. For m > 0 with x ≤ 0 (left half-plane): also y = mx + b. For m > 0 with x > 0 (right half-plane): y = (m/2)x + b. The bend at x = 0 is continuous since both pieces give y = b there. This is the minimal perturbation of Euclidean lines that breaks Desargues while preserving every affine plane axiom (two points determine a unique line, two non-parallel lines meet, parallel postulate).

mainTheorems.name: MoultonCollinear
mainTheorems.description: Three-point Moulton collinearity: either all three points share an x-coordinate (vertical line) or they all lie on some non-vertical Moulton line specified by left-slope m and intercept b. The disjunction is critical: vertical lines are not in the range of onMoultonLine since they have undefined slope, so they need separate treatment. This shape directly drives the three-case structure of desargues_fails: vertical, m ≤ 0, m > 0.

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OAA'
mainTheorems.description: First perspectivity-from-O fact. Line OA has slope -3/2 ≤ 0, so it is an ordinary Moulton line (the bending only affects positive slopes). norm_num closes each of the three incidence checks O, A, A' under the negative-slope branch.

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OBB'
mainTheorems.description: Second perspectivity-from-O fact, and the one where Moulton bending becomes operationally visible inside the perspectivity hypothesis: line OB has left-slope 2/3 > 0. O = (0,0) is on the seam (onML_pos_left, since 0 ≤ 0), while B = (3,1) and B' = (9,3) are on the right half (onML_pos_right with right-slope 1/3). All three incidence checks discharge by norm_num.

mainTheorems.name: collinear_OCC'
mainTheorems.description: Third perspectivity-from-O fact, dispatched by the vertical-line branch of MoultonCollinear: O, C, C' all have x = 0. This is the case where the disjunctive structure of MoultonCollinear (vertical OR non-vertical Moulton line) is genuinely needed — no single non-vertical Moulton line could contain all three points.

mainTheorems.name: PQR_x_distinct
mainTheorems.description: Excludes the vertical case from desargues_fails. The three intersection points P=(-17,9), Q=(27,17), R=(-6,11) have pairwise distinct x-coordinates (-17 ≠ 27 ≠ -6 ≠ -17), so no vertical Moulton line can contain all three. This lemma is what the vertical branch of desargues_fails dispatches against, leaving only the genuine algebraic case (m ≤ 0 or m > 0) for the linarith / linear_combination machinery.
mainTheorems.leanType: P_pt.1 ≠ Q_pt.1 ∧ P_pt.1 ≠ R_pt.1 ∧ Q_pt.1 ≠ R_pt.1

sections.title: Overview: Non-Desarguesian Planes and the Moulton Construction
sections.summary: The file docstring states the open question — can a non-Desarguesian projective/affine plane be formalized in Lean to exhibit Desargues's theorem *failing*? — and answers it with the **Moulton plane** (Forest Ray Moulton, 1902). The construction modifies the real affine plane $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ by *bending* every positive-slope line at the $y$-axis: a line with left-slope $m > 0$ keeps slope $m$ for $x \le 0$ but halves to slope $m/2$ for $x > 0$, while vertical lines and lines of slope $m \le 0$ are left ordinary. The resulting incidence structure still satisfies all affine-plane axioms (two points determine a unique line, parallels exist and are unique) yet violates Desargues's theorem, proving that Desargues is *independent* of the affine axioms and cannot be derived without additional algebraic (field/division-ring coordinatization) structure. The docstring also tabulates the explicit rational counterexample certified below: centre of perspectivity $O = (0,0)$; triangles $A=(-2,3), B=(3,1), C=(0,-1)$ and $A'=(-4,6), B'=(9,3), C'=(0,-4)$; corresponding-side intersections $P=(-17,9)$, $Q=(27,17)$, $R=(-6,11)$. These three points are Euclidean-collinear (classical Desargues holds in $\mathbb{R}^2$) but **not** Moulton-collinear, which is exactly the failure the formalization makes machine-checkable.
sections.mathContext: Moulton line ($m>0$): $y = m x + b$ for $x \le 0$, $y = \tfrac{m}{2} x + b$ for $x > 0$. Independence result: $\text{affine axioms} \not\vdash \text{Desargues}$.

sections.title: Part I: Moulton Line Definition and Helpers
sections.summary:
Establishes the core data structures of the Moulton plane through a piecewise predicate and a disjunctive collinearity relation, plus six gateway lemmas that bridge predicate-form goals and equation-form hypotheses across the slope-sign / half-plane case split.

**`onMoultonLine m b P` (lines 50-58)** — the piecewise membership predicate, defined by a two-level Classical if-then-else: when `m ≤ 0` it reduces to the ordinary line equation $P_y = m P_x + b$; when `m > 0` it splits on the sign of $P_x$, giving $P_y = m P_x + b$ on the left half-plane ($P_x \leq 0$) and $P_y = \tfrac{m}{2} P_x + b$ on the right half-plane ($P_x > 0$). The construction is the minimal continuous piecewise-linear perturbation of Euclidean lines: both pieces agree at $x = 0$ (giving $y = b$), so a Moulton line with $m > 0$ traces an unbroken bent curve whose slope halves as it crosses the $y$-axis from left to right. The `open Classical` at line 46 enables `Decidable (m ≤ 0)` for use inside the if-then-else on Prop — without it the definition would not even type-check, since the slope-sign case split is not decidable in Lean's constructive default.

**`MoultonCollinear P Q R` (lines 60-62)** — three-point collinearity, defined disjunctively: either all three points share an $x$-coordinate (the vertical-line case, $P_x = Q_x = R_x$, which `onMoultonLine` cannot capture since vertical lines have undefined slope) OR there exist $m, b \in \mathbb{R}$ such that all three points lie on the Moulton line $(m, b)$. This disjunction directly drives the three-case structure of `desargues_fails` downstream: the proof of $\neg \mathrm{MoultonCollinear}\ P\ Q\ R$ must refute both disjuncts, producing the vertical / $m \leq 0$ / $m > 0$ trichotomy that the rest of Part V navigates.

**Six helper lemmas (lines 66-88)** — three constructors (`onML_neg_slope`, `onML_pos_left`, `onML_pos_right`) and three extractors (`onML_eq_neg`, `onML_eq_pos_left`, `onML_eq_pos_right`), each handling one branch of the if-then-else. The constructors take an explicit branch hypothesis (e.g. `hm : m ≤ 0` or `hx : P.1 ≤ 0`) plus the equation that branch claims, and produce `onMoultonLine m b P`. The extractors reverse the direction: from `onMoultonLine m b P` plus the same branch hypotheses they recover the equation. The split is not just stylistic — by exposing the equation form, the extractors let `linarith` and `linear_combination` work on bare linear equalities in `m, b` rather than having to unfold the if-then-else inside an arithmetic tactic. All six lemmas have one-line proofs (`simp only [onMoultonLine, …]; exact h`) and exist purely to keep downstream proofs tactic-flat: every later incidence proof in Parts III-IV cites exactly one of these six lemmas plus one `norm_num` for the equation check.

sections.title: Part II: Counterexample Data Points
sections.summary:
Declares the ten rational-coordinate points that drive the entire counterexample as `private def`s in $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, deliberately chosen so that (a) the perspectivity hypothesis is geometrically transparent and (b) the resulting Moulton-line intersections $P, Q, R$ separate over the $y$-axis into a configuration that the bent-line definition can detect.

**Perspectivity witnesses** — $O = (0, 0)$ as the centre, $A = (-2, 3)$, $B = (3, 1)$, $C = (0, -1)$ as the first triangle, and $A' = (-4, 6)$, $B' = (9, 3)$, $C' = (0, -4)$ as the second. The scalar relationships $A' = 2A$, $B' = 3B$, $C' = 4C$ are not merely coincidental — they make the perspectivity from $O$ algebraically immediate: $O$, $A$, $A'$ are forced collinear because $A' - O = 2(A - O)$, so the three points lie on the ray from $O$ through $A$, and analogously for the other two corresponding pairs. The scaling factors $2, 3, 4$ are deliberately *distinct* (rather than the simpler choice $A' = 2A$, $B' = 2B$, $C' = 2C$): when the scaling factors coincide, the two triangles are homothetic from $O$ with the same dilation factor, and the corresponding sides $AB \parallel A'B'$, $BC \parallel B'C'$, $CA \parallel C'A'$ become parallel — sending the intersection points $P, Q, R$ to infinity in the affine plane and forcing Desargues to hold in a *degenerate* sense (the three intersections lie on the line at infinity, which is collinear by convention). Distinct scaling factors place $P, Q, R$ at finite, computable rational positions where the Moulton-bending distinction becomes operationally testable.

**Intersection witnesses** — $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$. The $x$-coordinates separate over the $y$-axis: $P_x = -17 < 0$ and $R_x = -6 < 0$ are on the left half-plane, while $Q_x = 27 > 0$ is on the right half-plane. This is the crucial geometric feature the bending exploits — any positive-slope Moulton line through $P$ and $R$ uses its unbent left-half equation, while the same line through $Q$ would use its halved-slope right-half equation, and these two regimes force inconsistent $(m, b)$ values when $P, Q, R$ are simultaneously asserted to be collinear. The downstream `desargues_fails` proof in Part V reduces exactly to extracting the linear system from the two regimes and showing it is over-determined ($11m = 2$ from $P, R$ vs $61m = 16$ from $P, Q$, which force $m = 2/11$ and $m = 16/61$ simultaneously — a $\frac{2}{11} \neq \frac{16}{61}$ contradiction). Marking all ten points as `private def` (rather than `def` or `notation`) confines the names to the `MoultonPlane` namespace and prevents accidental re-export; the points are pure proof scaffolding, not part of the public API of the formalization.

sections.title: Part III: Perspectivity from O
sections.summary:
Establishes the *perspectivity* hypothesis of Desargues's theorem inside the Moulton plane: triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are perspective from $O = (0,0)$, i.e. the three lines $OA A'$, $OB B'$, $OC C'$ are each Moulton-collinear. Each of the three lemmas exercises a different branch of the disjunctive `MoultonCollinear` predicate, and together they exhibit the full taxonomy of Moulton-collinear configurations the bent-line structure admits.

**`collinear_OAA'` (lines 108-115)** — line $OA$ has slope $\tfrac{3 - 0}{-2 - 0} = -\tfrac{3}{2} \leq 0$, so by the negative-slope branch of `onMoultonLine` it is just the ordinary Euclidean line $y = -\tfrac{3}{2} x$. The proof picks `m = -3/2`, `b = 0` for the existential in the non-vertical disjunct of `MoultonCollinear`, then discharges each of the three incidence checks with `onML_neg_slope (by norm_num) _ (by simp [..]; ring)`: `norm_num` confirms $-\tfrac{3}{2} \leq 0$ and `ring` closes the linear equation after unfolding the point definitions. The Moulton bending is *invisible* here — the line lives entirely in the negative-slope regime where ordinary Euclidean geometry applies.

**`collinear_OBB'` (lines 117-124)** — line $OB$ has slope $\tfrac{1}{3} > 0$, so the Moulton bending is operationally relevant. The proof picks `m = 2/3` as the *left-slope*: on the left half-plane the line has slope $2/3$, on the right half-plane it has the halved slope $\tfrac{2/3}{2} = \tfrac{1}{3}$ (matching the Euclidean slope of $OB$). $O = (0, 0)$ lies on the seam at $x = 0$ — it satisfies the left branch since $0 \leq 0$ — and the proof discharges it with `onML_pos_left`. $B = (3, 1)$ and $B' = (9, 3)$ are both on the right half ($B_x = 3 > 0$, $B'_x = 9 > 0$), so they use `onML_pos_right` with the halved-slope equation $1 = \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot 3 + 0$ and $3 = \tfrac{1}{3} \cdot 9 + 0$, both closed by `ring`. This lemma is the *only* place in the perspectivity proof where the bent-line definition is genuinely exercised, and demonstrates that the choice of $m = 2/3$ left-slope (rather than $m = 1/3$, which would be the Euclidean slope) is the correct way to describe a positive-slope Moulton line — the parameter $m$ in `onMoultonLine` is always the *left* slope, with the right slope inferred as $m/2$ by the piecewise definition.

**`collinear_OCC'` (lines 126-129)** — line $OC$ is vertical: $O = (0, 0)$, $C = (0, -1)$, $C' = (0, -4)$ all have $x = 0$. The proof selects the first disjunct of `MoultonCollinear` (the vertical case) and discharges the two equality conjuncts $0 = 0 \wedge 0 = 0$ by `simp` after unfolding the point definitions. This lemma exercises the case that `onMoultonLine` cannot capture — vertical lines have undefined slope in any slope-intercept formalism, so the disjunctive definition of `MoultonCollinear` is genuinely necessary; without the vertical disjunct, this perspectivity fact would be unprovable and the entire counterexample construction would collapse. Together, the three lemmas show that the Moulton-collinearity relation faithfully captures *every* configuration of three collinear points: ordinary negative-slope lines, bent positive-slope lines, and vertical lines.

sections.title: Part IV: Intersection Points
sections.summary:
Verifies the eighteen incidence facts that pin $P = (-17, 9)$, $Q = (27, 17)$, $R = (-6, 11)$ as the Moulton-line intersections of corresponding sides — six lemmas per intersection point, asserting that each of $P, Q, R$ lies on both of its two relevant corresponding-side Moulton lines and that all six endpoints ($A, B, A', B'$ for $P$; $B, C, B', C'$ for $Q$; $C, A, C', A'$ for $R$) lie on the corresponding lines they should.

**$P$ block (lines 139-160, six lemmas)** — Both $AB$ (slope $\tfrac{1-3}{3-(-2)} = -\tfrac{2}{5}$, intercept $\tfrac{11}{5}$) and $A'B'$ (slope $\tfrac{3-6}{9-(-4)} = -\tfrac{3}{13}$, intercept $\tfrac{66}{13}$) have negative slope, so they are *ordinary* Moulton lines — the bending never engages. `P_on_AB`, `A_on_AB`, `B_on_AB`, `P_on_A'B'`, `A'_on_A'B'`, `B'_on_A'B'` each invoke `onML_neg_slope (by norm_num) _ (by simp [..]; ring)`, with `norm_num` confirming the slope is $\leq 0$ and `ring` discharging the equation after unfolding the point coordinates. The arithmetic is entirely rational: e.g. $9 = -\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot (-17) + \tfrac{11}{5} = \tfrac{34}{5} + \tfrac{11}{5} = \tfrac{45}{5} = 9$. ✓

**$Q$ block (lines 164-186, six lemmas)** — The *only* block where the Moulton bending becomes genuinely operative. Both sides $BC$ (left-slope $\tfrac{4}{3}$, intercept $-1$, right-slope $\tfrac{2}{3}$ matching the Euclidean slope $BC$ has when measured between $B = (3, 1)$ at $x > 0$ and $C = (0, -1)$ at $x = 0$) and $B'C'$ (left-slope $\tfrac{14}{9}$, intercept $-4$, right-slope $\tfrac{7}{9}$) have positive slope, so the bent definition matters. $Q = (27, 17)$ is at $x = 27 > 0$ — right half-plane — so `Q_on_BC` and `Q_on_B'C'` invoke `onML_pos_right` with the *halved-slope* equations $17 = \tfrac{4/3}{2} \cdot 27 + (-1) = \tfrac{2}{3} \cdot 27 - 1 = 18 - 1 = 17$ ✓ and $17 = \tfrac{14/9}{2} \cdot 27 + (-4) = \tfrac{7}{9} \cdot 27 - 4 = 21 - 4 = 17$ ✓. Meanwhile $B = (3, 1)$ and $B' = (9, 3)$ are also on the right half (both have $x > 0$), so `B_on_BC` and `B'_on_B'C'` use `onML_pos_right`, while $C = (0, -1)$ and $C' = (0, -4)$ are on the seam $x = 0 \leq 0$ and use `onML_pos_left` with the *unbent* slope. This block exhibits a subtle but crucial feature of the bent-line definition: the parametrisation is by *left-slope*, not Euclidean slope, so the apparent left-slope $\tfrac{4}{3}$ for side $BC$ is consistent with the Euclidean slope $\tfrac{2}{3}$ measured on the right half — and the choice of parametrisation is forced by the requirement that incidence checks for $B$ on the right half and $C$ on the seam both go through.

**$R$ block (lines 188-210, six lemmas)** — Symmetric to $P$: both $CA$ (slope $\tfrac{3-(-1)}{-2-0} = -2$, intercept $-1$) and $C'A'$ (slope $\tfrac{6-(-4)}{-4-0} = -\tfrac{5}{2}$, intercept $-4$) have negative slope, so they are ordinary Moulton lines and the bending is invisible. `R_on_CA`, `C_on_CA`, `A_on_CA`, `R_on_C'A'`, `C'_on_C'A'`, `A'_on_C'A'` all use `onML_neg_slope` with `ring`-discharged equations: e.g. $11 = -2 \cdot (-6) + (-1) = 12 - 1 = 11$. ✓ The systematic asymmetry between the $P, R$ blocks (ordinary) and the $Q$ block (bent) is the proof-architectural reason the bending becomes detectable: $P$ and $R$ are computed by classical $\mathbb{R}^2$ linear algebra (unaware of the bend), while $Q$'s position is forced by the halved-slope right-half equations — so when the proof of $\neg \mathrm{MoultonCollinear}\ P\ Q\ R$ in Part V tries to fit a single Moulton line through all three, the regime mismatch (left-half slope for $P, R$ vs right-half slope for $Q$) produces the algebraic inconsistency. Without the bend, $P, Q, R$ would be Euclidean-collinear (and indeed they are, with Euclidean slope $\tfrac{2}{11}$) and Desargues's theorem would hold.

sections.title: Part V: Desargues Fails — ¬ MoultonCollinear P Q R
sections.summary:
The technical heart of the formalization: a 35-line tactic-mode proof that the three intersection points $P, Q, R$ are *not* Moulton-collinear, refuting the conclusion of Desargues's theorem in the Moulton plane after Parts II-IV have verified its hypothesis (perspectivity from $O$). The proof structure mirrors the disjunctive definition of `MoultonCollinear` exactly — `rcases h with ⟨hv1, _⟩ | ⟨m, b, hP, hQ, hR⟩` peels off the vertical case, then `by_cases hm : m ≤ 0` splits the non-vertical case by slope sign, giving the three-leaf contradiction tree.

**Setup (lines 227-229)** — `PQR_x_distinct` is a private helper that records $-17 \neq 27 \wedge -17 \neq -6 \wedge 27 \neq -6$ as a single conjunction, closed by `simp [P_pt, Q_pt, R_pt]; norm_num`. Although the main theorem inlines its first conjunct directly rather than citing the helper, the lemma documents the geometric fact (distinct $x$-coordinates) that excludes vertical collinearity.

**Vertical leaf (lines 235-238)** — From the first disjunct, `hv1 : P.1 = Q.1` unfolds to $-17 = 27$, immediately closed by `norm_num`. The two-conjunct `hv1, _` pattern discards the redundant $P.1 = R.1$ since a single inequality suffices for refutation.

**$m \leq 0$ leaf (lines 240-246)** — Extracts the ordinary-line equations $9 = m \cdot (-17) + b$ (`hP'`) and $17 = m \cdot 27 + b$ (`hQ'`) via `onML_eq_neg`. Subtracting gives $17 - 9 = m \cdot 27 - m \cdot (-17)$, i.e. $8 = 44m$, hence $m = \tfrac{2}{11} > 0$ — but the case hypothesis is $m \leq 0$, so this is a direct contradiction closed by `linarith`. Geometrically, this case captures the Euclidean truth that $P, Q$ have positive slope $\tfrac{17 - 9}{27 - (-17)} = \tfrac{8}{44} = \tfrac{2}{11}$, which no negative-slope line can match.

**$m > 0$ leaf (lines 247-261)** — The most intricate case, where the bent-line structure does the work. Three branch hypotheses are first established by `norm_num`: $P.1 = -17 \leq 0$ (left half), $Q.1 = 27 > 0$ (right half), $R.1 = -6 \leq 0$ (left half). The three extractors then produce the three equations: $9 = m \cdot (-17) + b$ via `onML_eq_pos_left`, $17 = \tfrac{m}{2} \cdot 27 + b$ via `onML_eq_pos_right` (note the halved slope!), and $11 = m \cdot (-6) + b$ via `onML_eq_pos_left`. The two `linear_combination` calls now do the algebraic work: `hP' - hR'` cancels $b$ and yields $-2 = (-17 + 6) m = -11m$, i.e. $11m = 2$ (`h1`); `2 * hP' - 2 * hQ'` cancels $b$ and the half-factor, yielding $18 - 34 = (-34 - 27) m$, i.e. $-16 = -61m$ or $61m = 16$ (`h2`). The final `linarith` closes the goal by detecting $61 \cdot 2 = 122 \neq 176 = 11 \cdot 16$ — equivalently, $m = \tfrac{2}{11}$ from `h1` and $m = \tfrac{16}{61}$ from `h2` are incompatible since $\tfrac{2}{11} = \tfrac{122}{671} \neq \tfrac{176}{671} = \tfrac{16}{61}$. The over-determination of the linear system in $(m, b)$ — three equations in two unknowns with no consistent solution under the bent-line regime — is the precise algebraic obstruction that Desargues's theorem encodes; the Moulton bending makes it visible because it forces $Q$'s equation to use a different slope coefficient than $P$ and $R$. The `linear_combination` tactic is the modern Mathlib-idiomatic replacement for hand-crafted `have h := …; ring`-style algebraic manipulations, and reduces what would otherwise be a 10-line ring derivation to two one-liners citing the exact linear combination of hypotheses needed.

sections.title: Part VI: Full Desargues Counterexample Certificate
sections.summary:
Packages the entire Moulton counterexample as a single machine-checkable theorem `moulton_counterexample`, whose statement (lines 268-287) is a 22-component conjunction explicitly listing every geometric fact required to assert that Desargues's theorem fails for this specific triangle pair, and whose proof (lines 288-295) is a single term-mode anonymous-constructor expression `⟨…⟩` citing the 22 lemmas proven in Parts III-V.

**Statement structure (lines 268-287)** — Decomposes into four blocks: (1) **perspectivity** — three conjuncts `MoultonCollinear O A A'`, `MoultonCollinear O B B'`, `MoultonCollinear O C C'` certifying that triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are in Moulton perspective from $O = (0, 0)$, the *hypothesis* of Desargues's theorem; (2) **first-triangle-side incidences** — six conjuncts asserting $P, A, B$ on line $AB$ (slope $-2/5$, intercept $11/5$) and $P, A', B'$ on line $A'B'$ (slope $-3/13$, intercept $66/13$), certifying that $P$ really is the intersection $AB \cap A'B'$; (3) **second-triangle-side incidences** — six conjuncts asserting $Q, B, C$ on line $BC$ (left-slope $4/3$, intercept $-1$) and $Q, B', C'$ on line $B'C'$ (left-slope $14/9$, intercept $-4$), the bent-line block; (4) **third-triangle-side incidences plus failure** — six conjuncts for $R$ on $CA$ and $C'A'$, then the *conclusion-negation* $\neg \mathrm{MoultonCollinear}\ P\ Q\ R$ as the final conjunct. The block structure encodes Desargues's theorem statement faithfully: hypothesis (perspectivity from a point) + intersection-defining incidences (which the standard statement leaves implicit but a formalization must spell out) + negation of the conclusion (corresponding-side intersections collinear). A reader checking the theorem need not trust any external claim about what $P, Q, R$ are — the incidence conjuncts pin them down as the unique Moulton-line intersections of the corresponding sides, so the negation `¬ MoultonCollinear P Q R` is genuinely asserting Desargues's failure rather than a trivial inequality of unrelated points.

**Proof (lines 288-295)** — A single anonymous-constructor term `⟨collinear_OAA', collinear_OBB', collinear_OCC', P_on_AB, A_on_AB, B_on_AB, P_on_A'B', A'_on_A'B', B'_on_A'B', Q_on_BC, B_on_BC, C_on_BC, Q_on_B'C', B'_on_B'C', C'_on_B'C', R_on_CA, C_on_CA, A_on_CA, R_on_C'A', C'_on_C'A', A'_on_C'A', desargues_fails⟩`. Lean's elaborator unifies each component with the corresponding conjunct in the statement, producing a term of the conjunction type without any tactic invocation. This is the canonical Lean 4 idiom for assembling a conjunctive theorem from already-proven pieces, and runs in O(n) elaboration time in the number of conjuncts — faster and more transparent than a tactic-mode proof using `refine ⟨?_, ?_, …⟩; exact …` or `constructor <;> exact …`. The result is a single named theorem that downstream Lean code (or external tools like Aristotle) can cite as `MoultonPlane.moulton_counterexample` to obtain the entire counterexample as a hypothesis — making the Moulton plane's failure of Desargues a *citable, machine-checkable* mathematical fact rather than an informal observation. This is the practical payoff of formalising a counterexample: future formalizations of the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization theorem can cite `moulton_counterexample` directly as the witness that the converse direction (every projective plane is Desarguesian) fails.

conclusion.summary: The Moulton plane provides a fully formalized, axiom-free counterexample to Desargues's theorem in an affine plane over ℝ. The explicit rational-coordinate construction (Moulton, 1902) proves that Desargues is NOT derivable from the affine plane axioms alone — it requires that the coordinatizing structure be a field or division ring. The formalization uses only Mathlib real arithmetic (norm_num, linarith, linear_combination) — no topology, continuity, or algebraic geometry.
conclusion.implications:
**Structural classification of projective planes.** The failure of Desargues's theorem characterises non-Desarguesian planes — those not coordinatizable by a skew field. Combined with the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization correspondence, the Moulton counterexample places projective planes into a strict hierarchy: **Pappian** (coordinatizable by a commutative field) $\subsetneq$ **Desarguesian** (coordinatizable by a skew field, possibly non-commutative) $\subsetneq$ **Moufang** (coordinatizable by an alternative algebra — adding the Cayley plane $\mathbb{O}\mathbb{P}^2$ as the unique non-Desarguesian Moufang plane) $\subsetneq$ **all projective planes** (coordinatizable only by a planar ternary ring). The Moulton plane is the historical and conceptual prototype of the bottom tier, and the gallery's `desargues-theorem-oq-01` (Desargues over commutative rings) and this entry (Moulton failure) together bracket the boundary between the top three tiers and the bottom one.

**Historical surprise and the rise of axiomatic geometry.** Moulton's 1902 counterexample was historically pivotal: most known plane geometries (Euclidean, hyperbolic, elliptic, all classical projective planes over fields) satisfied Desargues, and it had been widely assumed to follow from the affine axioms. Moulton's 4-page paper closed a question David Hilbert had opened only three years earlier in *Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899). The discovery accelerated the program of asking, for each classical theorem, *which* axioms it actually requires — a question that ultimately produced Hessenberg's 1905 theorem (Pappus $\Rightarrow$ Desargues), Hall's 1943 finite non-Desarguesian planes, and the full Hilbert-Hall coordinatization correspondence between geometric incidence properties and algebraic structures on the coordinatizing ring.

**Connections to the algebraic structure of coordinate rings.** Combined with `desargues-theorem-oq-01` (which proves Desargues over any commutative ring via homogeneous coordinates), this entry provides the complete picture: Desargues holds in coordinate planes over commutative rings (in particular over fields), and fails in planes whose coordinatization requires genuinely non-associative or non-distributive structures. The non-associativity of multiplication in the Moulton plane's coordinatizing ternary ring is *the precise algebraic reason* Desargues fails — recovered formally by the Hilbert-Hall theorems but visible concretely in the 3-case linear-algebra contradiction at the heart of `desargues_fails`. This is a paradigmatic instance of the geometry-algebra dictionary that Hilbert pioneered: every shift in the axiomatic structure of the projective plane corresponds to a shift in the algebraic structure of its coordinatizing ring, and vice versa.

**Tractability for formal verification.** The Lean 4 proof at the 300-line scale demonstrates that combinatorial-geometric counterexamples involving piecewise-defined incidence relations, rational-coordinate calculations, and finite case analysis on slope sign are tractable with modern tactic automation. Five tactics — `norm_num`, `linarith`, `linear_combination`, `by_cases`, and `simp` — close every goal in the formalization. No topology, continuity, or algebraic geometry machinery is invoked; the proof works entirely in the elementary algebra of $\mathbb{Q}$-rational points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. This makes the Moulton plane a particularly clean target for foundational geometry formalization, and suggests that the larger Hilbert-Hall classification program (Pappian / Desarguesian / Moufang / general) is within reach of similar elementary techniques once the appropriate definitions are in place.
openQuestions: Can the Moulton plane be extended to a full *projective* plane by adjoining a line at infinity, and Desargues's failure transferred to the projective completion? The standard construction projectivises an affine plane $\mathcal{A}$ by adding one new point per parallelism class of lines (the 'point at infinity' of that class) plus a new 'line at infinity' containing all the new points; the resulting structure $\mathbb{P}\mathcal{A}$ is a projective plane iff $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies the affine axioms. For the Moulton plane the construction is nontrivial because the parallelism relation must be defined modulo the bending — two Moulton lines should be 'parallel' iff their left-slopes agree (the right-slopes follow by halving). Once the projectivisation is carried out, the question is whether the affine Desargues failure proven here (two triangles in perspective from a point, intersections not collinear) lifts to a projective Desargues failure (two triangles in projective perspective, intersections not on a common projective line). This is expected by general principles — affine and projective Desargues are equivalent for any affine plane sitting inside its projective completion — but a Lean formalization would require defining the projective Moulton plane, the embedding $\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}\mathcal{A}$, and proving the equivalence of affine and projective Desargues, then exhibiting `moulton_counterexample` as the witness on the affine side. A natural follow-up gallery entry, and a useful test case for any Lean-formalized theory of projective completions of affine planes.

Can the smallest finite non-Desarguesian projective plane — the **Hall plane of order 9** (Marshall Hall, Jr., 1943) — be formalized in Lean as a sibling to this Moulton entry? The Hall plane has $9^2 + 9 + 1 = 91$ points and 91 lines, and is coordinatised by the *Dickson nearfield* of order 9: the set $\mathbb{F}_9$ equipped with a modified multiplication that twists by the Frobenius automorphism on one half of the elements, producing a structure that satisfies all field axioms except the left-distributive law (which holds only conditionally). The Hall construction proceeds by taking a 'Bruck-Bose spread' of disjoint lines in $\mathbb{P}^3(\mathbb{F}_3)$, identifying parallel classes via a non-linear involution, and reconstructing a projective plane whose ternary ring is the Dickson nearfield. Formalising this in Lean would require (a) defining Dickson nearfields and proving the relevant identities, (b) defining the André-Bruck-Bose construction for finite affine translation planes, (c) computing the 91 lines explicitly (each as a 10-element subset of the 91 points), and (d) proving that Desargues fails by exhibiting an explicit triangle-pair counterexample — most likely via computer-checked enumeration since the Hall plane's incidence structure is too irregular for purely symbolic case analysis. The payoff would be a finite, fully-discrete counterexample sibling to the present continuous Moulton entry, bracketing the finite/infinite divide and the role of Wedderburn's little theorem in obstructing finite *Desarguesian-but-not-Pappian* planes (none exist, by Wedderburn) while permitting finite non-Desarguesian ones (Hall, Hughes, André families).

Can the *converse* coordinatization theorem be formalized: a projective plane satisfies Desargues's theorem if and only if it is coordinatisable by a *skew field* (division ring)? This is Hilbert's 1899 theorem (*Grundlagen* §§22-30), refined by Hall (1943) and Veblen-Young (1910). One direction — every projective plane over a skew field $D$ (with points $D^3 \setminus \{0\} / D^\times$ and lines kernels of $D$-linear functionals) is Desarguesian — is essentially what the gallery's `desargues-theorem-oq-01` proves over an arbitrary commutative ring, and a careful re-reading of that proof would show it extends to non-commutative $D$ verbatim once `Comm` is dropped. The harder direction — every Desarguesian projective plane $\Pi$ admits a coordinate skew field — is Hilbert's *Streckenrechnung* (calculus of line segments): starting from $\Pi$ plus a choice of four 'frame' points in general position, one defines addition and multiplication of 'lengths' along a single line using carefully chosen Desargues configurations to verify the field axioms. Each axiom — associativity of addition, associativity of multiplication, distributivity, existence of inverses — corresponds to one specific Desargues configuration, and the construction collapses into one of Hall's planar ternary rings whose ternary operation is shown to factor as $T(x, y, z) = xy + z$ with $(+, \cdot)$ a skew field. A Lean formalization would require (i) defining abstract projective planes (incidence-only, no coordinates), (ii) implementing the Streckenrechnung as an inductive construction on point configurations, (iii) verifying each field axiom via the relevant Desargues invocation, and (iv) proving uniqueness up to isomorphism. The Hilbert-Moufang loop construction (and its modern Stevenhagen-Stoltzfus refinement) gives a cleaner alternative path through quasigroup theory but introduces additional algebraic infrastructure. Either way, this is a serious mid-scale formalization project (~5000-10000 lines) that would put projective plane theory on the same Lean-formalised footing as group theory.

Can the 1-parameter family of bent-line affine planes $\mathrm{Moulton}_\lambda$ — defined by the piecewise rule slope $m$ for $x \leq 0$ and slope $\lambda m$ for $x > 0$ when $m > 0$, with $\lambda \in (0,1)$ — be classified up to isomorphism, and the moduli space $\{ \lambda \in (0,1) \} / \sim$ formalized in Lean? KeyInsight #9 observes that every $\lambda \in (0,1)$ produces a non-Desarguesian plane and that $\lambda = 1/2$ is Moulton's canonical rational choice; the natural follow-up is whether the resulting planes are pairwise non-isomorphic (so the bent-plane moduli space is genuinely 1-dimensional), pairwise isomorphic (so $\lambda = 1/2$ is canonical up to relabelling and the moduli space is a point), or stratify into countably-many isomorphism classes indexed by an algebraic invariant of $\lambda$ (e.g. its $\mathbb{Q}$-conjugacy class under field automorphisms when $\lambda$ is algebraic). A formalization would require defining isomorphism of affine planes via incidence-preserving bijections, computing the planar ternary ring (PTR) of $\mathrm{Moulton}_\lambda$ as a function of $\lambda$, and exhibiting either a continuous family of isomorphisms (collapsing moduli) or a $\lambda$-distinguishing invariant (separating moduli) — a research direction at the intersection of incidence geometry and Lean-formalized algebraic structure theory.

references.title: A Simple Non-Desarguesian Plane Geometry
references.author: Forest Ray Moulton
references.journal: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
references.note: The original 4-page paper introducing the Moulton plane — written while Moulton was a graduate student of E. H. Moore at the University of Chicago. The construction uses the points of ℝ² with positive-slope lines bent at the y-axis (right-half slope halved), and exhibits an explicit non-Desarguesian configuration.

references.title: Grundlagen der Geometrie
references.author: David Hilbert
references.note: The foundational text establishing the axiomatic method in modern geometry. §§22–30 develop the coordinatization of Desarguesian projective planes by skew fields: every Desarguesian plane admits a unique-up-to-isomorphism skew field as coordinate ring (Hilbert's coordinatization theorem), and conversely projective planes over skew fields are Desarguesian. Hilbert's program of asking which axioms each classical theorem depends on directly motivated Moulton's 1902 counterexample.

references.title: Beweis des Desarguesschen Satzes aus dem Pascalschen
references.author: Gerhard Hessenberg
references.note: Proved that Pappus's theorem (here called 'Pascal's theorem' in the conic-degenerate case) implies Desargues's theorem in any projective plane. This established the strict hierarchy Pappian ⊊ Desarguesian among projective planes, and showed that the Moulton plane — being non-Desarguesian — must also be non-Pappian. The converse (Desarguesian ⇒ Pappian) fails: the real quaternions ℍ coordinatize a Desarguesian-but-non-Pappian plane.

references.title: Projective Planes
references.author: Marshall Hall, Jr.
references.journal: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
references.note: Constructed the first finite non-Desarguesian projective plane — the Hall plane of order 9 (91 points, 91 lines), coordinatized by a non-associative nearfield of order 9 (Dickson 1905). The paper also introduced planar ternary rings (PTRs) as the universal coordinatizing structure for arbitrary projective planes, establishing the full algebraic hierarchy: PTR (general) → alternative algebra (Moufang) → skew field (Desarguesian) → commutative field (Pappian).

references.title: A System of Axioms for Geometry
references.author: Oswald Veblen
references.journal: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
references.note: Veblen's foundational axiomatization of projective geometry. Together with the Veblen-Young book *Projective Geometry* (vol. 1, 1910), established that in projective spaces of dimension ≥ 3, Desargues's theorem follows automatically from the incidence axioms — so non-Desarguesian behaviour is intrinsically a plane phenomenon. This is the dimension-2 vs dimension-≥3 dichotomy that makes the Moulton construction necessarily 2-dimensional.

references.title: Projective Planes
references.author: D. R. Hughes and F. C. Piper
references.venue: Springer Graduate Texts in Mathematics, vol. 6
references.note: Standard modern reference on the theory of projective planes — including Desarguesian, Moufang, and non-Desarguesian constructions, the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization theory via planar ternary rings, and the finite-plane existence problem (Bruck-Ryser, Lam-Thiel-Swiercz). Provides the textbook treatment of the Moulton plane and its place in the broader classification.

references.title: A Theorem on Finite Algebras
references.author: Joseph H. M. Wedderburn
references.journal: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society
references.note: Wedderburn's little theorem: **every finite division ring is a field** (i.e., multiplication in any finite skew field is automatically commutative). Combined with the Hilbert-Hall coordinatization correspondence — every Desarguesian projective plane is coordinatizable by a skew field, every Pappian projective plane by a commutative field — Wedderburn's theorem immediately implies that **every finite Desarguesian projective plane is automatically Pappian**. This is the structural reason why the strict containment Pappian $\subsetneq$ Desarguesian (which holds in general, witnessed by the real quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ coordinatizing a Desarguesian-but-non-Pappian plane $\mathbb{H}\mathbb{P}^2$) collapses for *finite* planes: in the finite setting, Desarguesian and Pappian are equivalent. Consequently, the *only* finite witnesses for the non-Desarguesian frontier are planes whose coordinatizing structure is genuinely non-associative — Hall planes (1943) coordinatized by Dickson nearfields, Hughes planes (1957), and the André planes (1954) — all of which require finite *nearfields* rather than division rings. The Moulton plane formalized in this entry, being an infinite plane over $\mathbb{R}$, sidesteps Wedderburn entirely: in the infinite setting, the bent-line trick produces a non-Desarguesian plane directly from a continuous deformation of the Euclidean coordinatization, with no finiteness obstruction. The interplay is structurally clean: Wedderburn explains *why* the Moulton-style trick must be infinite-dimensional (no finite analogue exists for the simplest case), while the Moulton construction itself reveals *how* non-Desarguesian behaviour emerges from genuinely non-associative coordinatization in the continuous setting. Wedderburn's original 1905 proof uses character theory of finite groups — specifically the conjugacy-class size formula in the multiplicative group of a finite division ring; later character-free proofs (Witt 1931, using cyclotomic polynomials) provide the textbook modern derivation. Cited in keyInsight #6 as the structural reason finite Desarguesian-but-non-Pappian planes do not exist.
